document_check.note: Berres M, Monsch AU, Spiegel R. Using historical data to facilitate clinical prevention trials in Alzheimer disease? An analysis of longitudinal MCI data sets. Alzheimer's Research & Therapy (2021) 13:97. It compares five MCI data sets (ADNI, NACC, InDDEx, CNG, BS-MC) on inclusion criteria, baseline data and later progression. This is the study the review cites, and the cited finding is in the abstract (p1) and discussion (p9).

cited_result: The five MCI samples were recruited under different criteria and had similar baseline cognitive scores, but later progression differed. The InDDEx trial sample showed about 10% progression to dementia at 4 years and did not decline on verbal fluency. The other four samples showed more than 30% progression; 3-year transition rates ranged from 5.9% (InDDEx) to 46.4% (NACC).
tool_reason: The cited result compares the incidence of progression to dementia, and cognitive change, across five descriptive samples. That makes it an incidence estimate per sample rather than a prediction model, a causal exposure effect or a systematic review (the 'meta-analysis' here pools individual data sets, with no literature search), so the JBI prevalence/incidence checklist fits best.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to address the target population
domains.rationale: The question is whether MCI samples assembled under different criteria differ. The five named data sets are the frames being compared, and a common age and education restriction was applied to all of them.

signalling.question: Was the sample frame appropriate to address the target population?
signalling.quote: We compared data from two North American cohort studies (n=395 and 4328, respectively), one company-sponsored international clinical drug trial (n=831) and two convenience patient samples, one from Germany (n=726), and one from Switzerland (n=1558).

domains.rationale: Two samples are convenience samples and only BS-MC is described as consecutive. Several data sets include patients who did not meet their own study's criteria, and the InDDEx sample was reduced for missing data.

signalling.question: Were study participants sampled in an appropriate way?
signalling.quote: It should also be mentioned that almost all datasets contain patients who did not fulfill one or more of their own study's inclusion and/or exclusion criteria (see comments to Table 3).

signalling.question: Was the sample size adequate?
signalling.quote: This left 4328 MCI subjects for our analysis.

domains.domain: 4. Subjects and setting described in detail
domains.rationale: Table 1 gives eligibility criteria and Table 3 gives demographics for each sample. Some NACC criteria are 'Not specified'.

signalling.question: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
signalling.quote: Patients in ADNI and NACC were oldest (74.2±7.5 and 74.4±7.9), those in InDDEx and BS-MC were younger (70.1±7.6 and 69.7±9.1), and CNG (68.0±7.9) comprised the youngest sample.

domains.rationale: Follow-up coverage differs sharply between the samples being compared (3-year drop-out from 25% to 98%), so the progression estimates rest on very different fractions of each sample.

signalling.question: Was the data analysis conducted with sufficient coverage of the identified sample?
signalling.quote: In the five studies considered, the rate of drop-outs after 3 years was quite different: 70% in NACC, 37% in ADNI, 25% in InDDEx, 77% in CNG, and 98% in BS-MC.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition (progression to dementia)
domains.rationale: Progression was a clinician's overall judgement at each visit. The paper does not name dementia criteria or say whether they were the same across the five sources.

signalling.question: Were valid methods used for the identification of the condition?
signalling.quote: In the five datasets considered, an overall judgement was provided at each patient visit by an experienced clinician as to whether the patient had progressed from MCI to dementia.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants
domains.rationale: Visit schedules, extra-visit ascertainment and test batteries all differed across samples, and the dementia criteria were not harmonised. The authors only assume the transition criteria were similar. The between-sample difference in progression may therefore partly reflect how progression was ascertained.

signalling.question: Was the condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants?
signalling.quote: Time to transition from MCI to dementia was usually ascertained at scheduled visits. Sometimes, however, patients were examined in an extra visit and then classified as being demented.

signalling.question: Was the ascertainment schedule comparable across samples?
signalling.quote: Figure 4 shows the pattern of event times for strict visit schedules of ADNI and InDDEx and less clearly for NACC and CNG.

domains.rationale: Kaplan-Meier estimates with standard errors, forest plots with heterogeneity statistics, and Cox models by study suit a descriptive comparison. The continuous-time assumption for interval-scheduled visits is acknowledged.

signalling.question: Was there appropriate statistical analysis?
signalling.quote: Transition rates after 3 years are between 5.9% (InDDEx) and 46.4% (NACC), both with a standard error of 1.1%.

domains.rationale: Attrition is very high in the convenience samples. It is discussed but not handled analytically; the authors only argue that the pattern does not support attrition bias.

signalling.question: Was the response rate adequate, and if not, was the low response rate managed appropriately?
signalling.quote: This factor may cause bias and could make studies less comparable.

overall: High risk of bias (by the review's JBI rule: item 7, standard and reliable measurement of the condition, is 'No')
overall_rationale: The cited contrast in progression between samples depends on dementia being ascertained comparably across five sources, and it was not: clinician judgement with unstated criteria, differing visit schedules, extra-visit diagnoses, different test batteries. It also depends on comparable follow-up, which ranged from 2% to 75% retention at 3 years with no analytical handling. The observed differences cannot be attributed to recruitment criteria rather than to ascertainment and attrition.
